name: Zaleplon
lead: Zaleplon, sold as Sonata, is a prescription nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic (pyrazolopyrimidine class) approved for short-term treatment of insomnia, particularly difficulty falling asleep.[1]

It acts at the BZ1 site of the GABA-A receptor and has a very short half-life of about one hour, which Grokipedia says reduces next-day effects.[1] It is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.[1]
It has no approved or studied appearance use. Its inclusion in this wiki reflects its place among sleep medicines discussed in recovery contexts.

paras: Zaleplon is indicated for short-term insomnia treatment taken immediately before bed when several hours of sleep are possible.[1][2] Its short half-life is described as suiting people who need to wake early.[1]

Common effects include headache, dizziness and somnolence; serious risks include complex sleep behaviors such as sleep-driving, anterograde amnesia, and dependence with prolonged use.[1][2] Dose reduction is advised for older people and those with hepatic impairment.[1]

A BMJ meta-analysis examined benefits and risks of short-term sedative hypnotics, including zaleplon, in older people with insomnia, covering sleep measures, adverse events and morning-after psychomotor impairment.[4] An earlier meta-analysis compared pharmacotherapy with behavioural therapy for persistent insomnia.[5] The AASM guideline and a Lancet network meta-analysis assess hypnotics for chronic insomnia.[3][6] A cohort study associated hypnotic use with higher mortality, though observational designs cannot show causation.[7] Pharmacological reviews describe the drug class.[8]
No studies of appearance outcomes were found.

card.summary: A short-acting prescription Z-drug sleeping pill (Sonata); no appearance data.
card.note: Schedule IV; complex sleep behaviors and dependence are labelled risks.

quick.overview:
Zaleplon (Sonata) is a prescription sleep medicine for short-term insomnia, notable for its roughly one-hour half-life.

It has not been studied for appearance.
quick.mechanism: It binds the BZ1 site on the GABA-A receptor, enhancing inhibitory signalling to induce sleep.
quick.risks: Reported effects include headache, dizziness, sleepiness, amnesia and complex sleep behaviors; dependence can occur with prolonged use. Schedule IV in the US.
